findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify that short_root teardown uses rmtree with a chmod-and-retry error handler for read-only files (as pytest's tmp cleanup does), and say whether residual failures are raised or logged.
evidence: "The fixture removes the root in a `finally`."
Absence: no mention of read-only file handling or of what happens when removal fails.
findings.finding: The teardown is only 'removes the root in a finally'. On Windows, git object and pack files are read-only, and plain shutil.rmtree raises PermissionError on them. The plan does not say how this is handled: an onerror/onexc chmod-and-retry like pytest's own tmp cleanup, or ignore_errors with a log. A teardown error would either fail the test on Windows or, if silently swallowed, leave tort-* directories in the system temp dir.
findings.location: Approach — 'The fixture removes the root in a finally'
scenarios: The nested run creates git repos under short_root. rmtree hits a read-only .git/objects file on Windows, and the fixture teardown errors so the test is reported as an error.
The removal error is suppressed, and tort-* directories pile up in the runner's temp dir across runs.
findings.suggested_fix: Use `shutil.rmtree(root, onerror=_make_writable_and_retry)`, with `onexc` on Python 3.12+. The handler runs `os.chmod(path, stat.S_IWRITE)` and then retries the failed function.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify that `short_root` teardown removes the tree with a Windows-safe rmtree that clears read-only bits and retries (or reuses pytest's tmp cleanup), so git's read-only object files do not error or leak on Windows.
evidence: "A new fixture `short_root` creates `tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="tort-")` directly under the system temp dir ... The fixture removes the root in a `finally`."
"git commit failed ... open("<id>/<event>-CREATE.json")" — the nested run creates git repos (ticket stores, job workspaces) under the sandbox and basetemp roots.

Platform fact: git on Windows writes loose and pack object files read-only. `shutil.rmtree` without an onerror/onexc handler raises PermissionError ([WinError 5]) on such files. pytest's tmp_path cleanup handles this case; a hand-rolled removal does not.
findings.finding: The new `short_root` fixture removes its root itself ('The fixture removes the root in a `finally`') instead of relying on pytest's tmp_path cleanup. On Windows, git creates read-only files under `.git/objects`. The nested basetemp holds ticket-store git repos. A plain `shutil.rmtree` fails on those files with PermissionError. pytest's own tmp_path cleanup avoids this by chmod-ing and retrying. The plan does not say how the removal handles read-only entries, or open handles left by lingering git or subprocess children.
findings.location: Approach — 'The fixture removes the root in a `finally`.'
scenarios: Windows (`sweep (windows)` on GitHub Actions): the nested run passes, but fixture teardown raises PermissionError while deleting `tort-*\r\...\.git\objects\...`. pytest reports the test as an ERROR at teardown, so AC2 is not met even though the MAX_PATH fix works.

Windows developer workstation: if removal is made `ignore_errors=True` to avoid that, each run leaves `tort-*` trees in %TEMP%. Nothing ever prunes them, because they sit outside pytest's retention-managed basetemp.
findings.suggested_fix: In the `finally`, call `shutil.rmtree(root, onexc=_force)` (or `onerror=` on Python <3.12). `_force` does `os.chmod(path, stat.S_IWRITE)` and then retries the failed function. State in the plan that teardown must not raise on Windows git read-only objects.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Say that `short_root` is removed with a Windows-safe rmtree that clears git's read-only bit and retries (reusing the `_clear_git_readonly_and_retry` onexc/onerror pattern), not a plain or `ignore_errors` rmtree. Also say that removal still fails loudly on any other error.
evidence: Plan: "The fixture removes the root in a `finally`."

findings.finding: The plan says the `short_root` fixture "removes the root in a `finally`" but does not say how. On Windows a plain `shutil.rmtree` fails on the read-only `.git/objects` files that the nested run leaves in both `t` (job workspaces, unless discard succeeded) and `r/nested-pytest` (the source stores of the nested tests, which pytest keeps under a given `--basetemp`). Teardown would then raise PermissionError and the test would error on exactly the platform it is meant to fix. If removal uses `ignore_errors=True` instead, private git trees pile up silently in the real system temp dir. Before this change, both trees sat under `tmp_path`, whose pytest cleanup tolerates read-only files. Moving them out removes that safety net.
findings.location: Approach — "The fixture removes the root in a `finally`"; tests/unit/test_opcert_key_copy_leak_tortoise.py
scenarios: Windows `sweep (windows)` run: the nested run passes and the leak assertion passes, then the fixture's `finally` rmtree hits a read-only pack/loose object under `short_root/r/nested-pytest/.../.git/objects`. PermissionError makes the test ERROR and AC2 is never met.

findings.finding: The `short_root` fixture creates the dir with `mkdtemp` and deletes it in a hand-written `finally`, limited to "tempfile and pathlib only". This rebuilds directory cleanup that `tempfile.TemporaryDirectory` and the repo's existing helpers already provide. It also drops the read-only-file handling that pytest's tmp_path teardown used to give for free. Pathlib has no recursive delete, so the plan either hand-rolls a recursive delete (NIH) or uses `shutil` (contradicting its own wording). A plain `rmtree` fails on Windows on the read-only git object files the nested run creates.
findings.location: Approach — "The fixture removes the root in a `finally` ... Portable: uses `tempfile` and `pathlib` only."
scenarios: On Windows the nested run leaves `.git/objects/*` files read-only under `short_root/r/nested-pytest/...`. A plain `shutil.rmtree` in the `finally` raises PermissionError, so the test errors at teardown even when the leak assertion passed.
A hand-written pathlib recursive delete that ignores errors silently leaves `tort-*` dirs in the runner's system temp. That is the same kind of temp-dir leak this test exists to catch.

findings.finding: The plan claims the new `short_root` fixture uses only `tempfile` and `pathlib` and removes its root in a `finally`. The repo contradicts this. That root will contain the nested pytest's basetemp (`short_root/r/nested-pytest`), and with an explicit --basetemp it is left on disk after the child exits. It holds the inner tests' git repos (authority/source stores) with git's read-only object files. The repo documents that on Windows a plain recursive delete of such a tree fails with PermissionError, and adds a chmod-and-retry handler for exactly this. On top of that, pathlib has no recursive delete, so the fixture would need `shutil` anyway.

findings.finding: The Cause section says git "is not built with `core.longpaths`". `core.longpaths` is a runtime git config setting in Git for Windows, not a build-time capability. Because the claim is wrong, the plan never checks or rules out the established alternative: setting `core.longpaths=true` for the nested run, e.g. through `GIT_CONFIG_COUNT`/`GIT_CONFIG_KEY_0`/`GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_0`. It also never points to the repo's earlier fix for the same failure (bug 09f9-6b9f).
scenarios: A future reader takes from the plan that long paths cannot be enabled for git, and misjudges later Windows path failures.
